title: Heritage sites in Karnataka: Hampi, Pattadakal and Hoysala temples
seo_title: Heritage Sites in Karnataka: UNESCO and Historical Places
meta_description: Heritage sites in Karnataka: UNESCO Hampi, Pattadakal and the Hoysala temples, plus Badami, Aihole, Vijayapura, Bidar, Shravanabelagola and Mysuru.
summary: Karnataka has three cultural UNESCO World Heritage Sites: Hampi (1986), Pattadakal (1987) and the Sacred Ensembles of the Hoysalas at Belur, Halebidu and Somanathapura (2023), plus parts of the Western Ghats (2012). Badami, Aihole, Vijayapura, Bidar, Kalaburagi, Shravanabelagola, Srirangapatna and Mysuru add Chalukya, Sultanate, Jain and royal layers.

sections.h2: Why Karnataka is a temple architecture classroom
paras: Few regions show the growth of Indian temple architecture as clearly as Karnataka. The Chalukyas of Badami (6th to 8th centuries) tried out northern and southern forms side by side at Aihole, Badami and Pattadakal. The Rashtrakutas, the later Chalukyas of Kalyani and the Hoysalas refined the regional style, and the [Vijayanagara empire](vijayanagara-empire.html) built one of the largest cities of its time at Hampi. The Bahmani and Adil Shahi sultans then gave the north of the state its domes and minarets.
Our session on [Deccan temple forms and the vesara debates](deccan-temple-forms-vesara-debates.html) explains why scholars still argue about how to classify these temples.

sections.h2: UNESCO World Heritage Sites in Karnataka
paras: Hampi (1986) was the capital of Vijayanagara from the 14th century until its sack after the battle of 1565. Its ruins spread over a boulder landscape on the Tungabhadra: the Virupaksha and Vitthala temples, the Royal Enclosure, the Lotus Mahal, stepped tanks and markets. See our [heritage walk in Hampi](heritage-walk-in-hampi.html) guide.

Pattadakal (1987) has a group of 7th and 8th-century Chalukya temples, including the Virupaksha temple built by a queen to celebrate a victory over the Pallavas, with northern and southern style towers side by side. Our [Pattadakal and Aihole programme](pattadakal-and-aihole-temple-design-laboratory.html) treats the two sites as a design laboratory.

The Sacred Ensembles of the Hoysalas (2023) comprise the Chennakeshava temple at Belur, the Hoysaleshvara temple at Halebidu and the Keshava temple at Somanathapura, built in the 12th and 13th centuries in soapstone with very fine carving on star-shaped plans. Parts of the Western Ghats (2012), a natural serial site, lie in Karnataka, including forest areas around Kudremukh and Talakaveri.

sections.h2: Ancient temples and caves beyond the UNESCO list
paras: Badami, the Chalukya capital Vatapi, has four rock-cut caves of the 6th century, three Brahmanical and one Jain, above an artificial lake, plus structural temples on the cliffs. Aihole has over a hundred temples, including the apsidal Durga temple and the Lad Khan temple, and an inscription of 634 CE by the poet Ravikirti for Pulakeshin II. See our [heritage walk in Badami](heritage-walk-in-badami.html) guide.

Shravanabelagola has the 57-foot monolithic Gommateshwara (Bahubali) statue, carved around 981 CE, and Jain inscriptions on Chandragiri hill that tradition connects with Chandragupta Maurya. Lakkundi, Ittagi and Kuruvatti have finely carved later Chalukya temples. Sannati, on the Bhima river, has Buddhist remains including a portrait relief long identified as Ashoka. The Ashokan edicts at Maski, Brahmagiri and Sannati are among the southernmost; Maski's edict, found in 1915, was the first to name the king as Asoka and not only by his title Devanampiya.

In the north, Kalaburagi (Gulbarga) was the first Bahmani capital, with a large mosque inside its fort. Bidar, the later capital, has the madrasa of Mahmud Gawan (1472) and the Bahmani tombs at Ashtur. Vijayapura (Bijapur), the Adil Shahi capital, has the Gol Gumbaz (completed 1656), one of the largest domes in the world, and the Ibrahim Rauza. See our [heritage walk in Vijayapura](heritage-walk-in-vijayapura.html) guide.

In the south, Srirangapatna was Tipu Sultan's island capital, with the Daria Daulat Bagh and the site of the 1799 siege. Mysuru has the Mysore Palace (rebuilt 1912), Chamundi Hill and the Wadiyar city plan; see [heritage walk in Mysuru](heritage-walk-in-mysuru.html).

sections.h2: How to read a Karnataka temple
paras: Karnataka's temples reward a slow, structured look. Start with the plan: Chalukya temples at Aihole are often simple squares or even apsidal, while Hoysala temples at Belur and Somanathapura use stellate, star-shaped plans that multiply the play of light and shadow on the walls. Then look at the tower. At Pattadakal you can compare the curved northern tower of the Papanatha temple with the stepped southern tower of the Virupaksha temple a few metres away.

Next, read the walls from bottom to top. Hoysala temples have horizontal friezes of elephants, lions, scrolls, horses and narrative scenes, then a band of large deity figures, then the eaves. The material matters too: soft chloritic schist (soapstone) let Hoysala sculptors cut deep, lace-like detail, while the sandstone of Badami and the granite of Hampi gave bolder, simpler forms.

Finally, look for inscriptions. Many temples carry records naming kings, queens, architects and donors. At Pattadakal an inscription names the queen Lokamahadevi as patron of the Virupaksha temple, and Hoysala sculptors sometimes signed their work, which gives a rare glimpse of individual artists. Our session on [temple sculpture and iconography](temple-sculpture-iconography.html) helps groups identify the deities and stories they will see.

sections.h2: Planning a heritage trip in Karnataka
paras: North Karnataka is best done as a circuit: Hampi, then Badami, Aihole and Pattadakal, then Vijayapura, ideally over five to seven days in the cooler months. The south circuit covers Mysuru, Srirangapatna, Somanathapura, Belur, Halebidu and Shravanabelagola from Bengaluru. Check the ASI website before you go.
Talaash Heritage runs a Pattadakal and Aihole programme and a multi-day South India temple architecture tour, and can build any other circuit as a study tour.

faq.q: How many UNESCO World Heritage Sites are in Karnataka?
faq.a: Three cultural sites lie wholly in Karnataka: Hampi (1986), Pattadakal (1987) and the Sacred Ensembles of the Hoysalas (2023). The state also shares the Western Ghats natural site (2012) with other states.

faq.q: Which are the best ancient temples in Karnataka?
faq.a: Pattadakal, Aihole and Badami for early Chalukya temples; Belur, Halebidu and Somanathapura for Hoysala work; Lakkundi for later Chalukya temples; and the Virupaksha and Vitthala temples at Hampi for Vijayanagara.
No. Badami's caves are not inscribed, though nearby Pattadakal is. Badami and Aihole are often visited with Pattadakal because together they show the full range of Chalukya temple building.

faq.q: Does Talaash Heritage run tours in Karnataka?
faq.a: Yes. We run a Pattadakal and Aihole programme and a multi-day South India temple architecture tour, and design custom study tours for any Karnataka circuit on request, from Hampi and Vijayapura in the north to the Hoysala temples in the south.

posts.hook: At Pattadakal, two styles stand side by side.
posts.caption: The 8th-century Chalukya builders put northern curved towers and southern stepped towers in the same complex. It reads like a design experiment.

posts.hook: At Halebidu, look at the bottom friezes.
posts.caption: The lowest bands of carving run in order: elephants, lions, scrolls, horses and stories. Follow one band around the temple.
